summary: This standards-track RFC introduces new sub-TLVs for IS-IS that carry prefix attribute flags for IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes, and the router ID of the router that originated a prefix advertisement.

eli5.summary: Each route announcement can now carry extra tags about itself and a note saying which router first announced it.

questions: what is the is-is x flag
what is the is-is n flag
what is an is-is source router id
what are is-is prefix attribute flags
subtitle: Three new IS-IS sub-TLVs that tag a route with extra flags and name the router that first announced it.

tldr.problem: The IPv4 and IPv6 reachability TLVs in IS-IS have fixed formats with no room for new flags, and when a route is leaked between levels, the original advertising router is no longer known.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV (X, R and N flags) and IPv4 and IPv6 Source Router ID sub-TLVs, all usable inside TLVs 135, 235, 236 and 237.
tldr.outcome: Routers can tell whether a prefix is external, re-advertised or a node address, and can tie node addresses back to one originating router ID. The RFC says this adds no new security concerns.

today: RFC 7794 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2016. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Prefixes Need Attributes
sections.content:
IS-IS is a link-state routing protocol. Earlier RFCs define extended ways to advertise IPv4 and IPv6 prefix reachability, but their formats are fixed, so new flags cannot be added without backwards compatibility problems.

The RFC gives two motivating cases. Knowing whether a prefix is directly connected to the advertising router matters for Segment Routing, because it decides how labels on an incoming packet are processed. Knowing which addresses identify a node is useful for services such as a Remote Loop Free Alternate (RLFA) endpoint.

A second problem is that when a router advertises several node addresses and they are leaked out of the area where they started, it helps to link them all to one Router ID. A new sub-TLV carries that Router ID.
sections.eli5: The old route announcements were like a form with no blank spaces left. This RFC adds a sticky note area so routers can say more about each route.

sections.title: The New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Three sub-TLVs are introduced: Prefix Attribute Flags, IPv4 Source Router ID and IPv6 Source Router ID. All of them apply to the extended reachability TLVs numbered 135, 235, 236 and 237.

The Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV has Type 4. Its Value is a variable number of bits (Length times 8), sent starting with bit 0. Future bits SHOULD be assigned in ascending order so that as few bits as possible need to be sent.
sections.eli5: There are three new kinds of sticker: one holding a row of yes-or-no switches, and two that name the router that started the announcement.

sections.title: The Attribute Flags
sections.content:
Three flags are defined. Undefined bits MUST be sent as 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt, and bits that are not transmitted MUST be treated as 0.

  • X-flag (External Prefix, bit 0): set if the prefix was redistributed from another protocol, including from another IS-IS instance. It MUST be preserved when leaked between levels. In TLVs 236 and 237 it SHOULD always be sent as 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt, because those TLVs already have an X flag in their fixed format.
  • R-flag (Re-advertisement, bit 1): set when the prefix has been leaked from one level to another, upwards or downwards.
  • N-flag (Node, bit 2): set when the prefix identifies the advertising router, meaning a host prefix for a globally reachable address, typically a loopback. A router MAY choose not to set it. If it is set on a prefix that is not a host prefix (/32 for IPv4, /128 for IPv6) it MUST be ignored, and it MUST be preserved when leaked between levels.
sections.eli5: The three switches say: 'I came from outside', 'I was passed along from another level', and 'this address belongs to the router itself'.

sections.title: Source Router ID
sections.content:
When a route is leaked from one level to another, the source of the original advertisement becomes unknown. The Source Router ID sub-TLVs fix that. The IPv4 version has Type 11 and Length 4. The IPv6 version has Type 12 and Length 16.

Including either one is optional and it MAY appear in TLVs 135, 235, 236 or 237. The value MUST be identical to the router ID in the Traffic Engineering router ID TLV 134 (IPv4) or the IPv6 TE Router ID TLV 140. If the sub-TLV is present, it MUST be included when the advertisement is leaked to another level.

The Router ID is always that of the IS-IS instance that originated the advertisement, even when the prefix was learned from another protocol and the X-flag is set.
sections.eli5: It is a name tag that stays on the announcement even when it is passed to a different neighbourhood, so everyone knows which router first said it.

sections.title: Advertising Router IDs
sections.content:
The earlier RFCs 5305 and 6119 define router ID advertisement for IPv4 and IPv6. Although they discuss it in the Traffic Engineering context, they explicitly allow router IDs to be advertised for other purposes. Identifying the source of a prefix is one such purpose.

Whenever a Source Router ID sub-TLV is used, the originating router SHOULD also advertise the matching address-family-specific router ID TLV.
sections.eli5: If you put a name tag on your announcement, you should also have your name posted on the board where people can look it up.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA adds the three sub-TLVs (values 4, 11 and 12) to the registry of sub-TLVs for TLVs 135, 235, 236 and 237. It also creates a new registry, "Bit Values for Prefix Attribute Flags Sub-TLV", under the "IS-IS TLV Codepoints" registry, with Expert Review as the registration policy. Bits 0, 1 and 2 are the X, R and N flags.

For security, the RFC points to the existing IS-IS authentication RFCs (RFC 5304 and RFC 5310) and states that advertising this additional information introduces no new security concerns.
sections.eli5: A public list keeps track of which sticker means what, and the authors say the stickers do not make routing any less safe.
